Neonates of the Red-billed Streamertail (Trochilus polytmus) emerge from the incubated bird egg at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet weight of just 0.56 grams [Ww0 = 0.56 grams]. This modest mass at hatching, a value typical of many hummingbird species, marks the beginning of an intensely rapid growth phase sustained entirely by biparental provisioning. Eggs incubating at 32 °C [T = 32 °C] exhibit a developmental period of approximately 18 days [ab = approximately 18 days], a figure that aligns with the 17 to 19 day range reported for other large-bodied trochilids and reflects the constrained thermal window necessary for successful organogenesis of the amniote embryo. The precise timing of hatching is closely tied to the thermal regime of the nest cup; deviations from this optimal incubation temperature often prolong the incubation period or reduce hatchling viability. Field measurements confirm that the 0.56 gram [Ww0 = 0.56 gram] neonate must nearly double its body mass within the first few days post-hatching to ensure sufficient thermoregulatory capacity, a challenge met by frequent crop-milk-like regurgitations from both attending parents during the altricial nestling stage.

The nestling chick period is characterized by a dramatic trajectory of somatic growth, culminating in the fledgling stage when the developing chick reaches a weight at fledging of 3.8 grams [Wwx = 3.8 grams]. This represents more than a sixfold increase from the hatchling mass, a metabolic feat driven by the high-quality insectivorous diet delivered by the parents. Under the thermal conditions typical of active life-history processes in this species (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]), the time since birth at fledging averages 21.5 days [tx = 21.5 days], though individual variation is observed with a range spanning 19 to 24 days depending on food availability and brood size. Once the fledgling achieves its first flight and nutritional independence, it enters the juvenile stage as a fully formed but still inexperienced young individual, gradually developing the foraging proficiency needed for survival. The attainment of this 3.8 gram [Wwx = 3.8 gram] fledgling mass is a critical developmental milestone, as it signals the completion of the most energetically vulnerable period of the life cycle.

Sexual maturation in Trochilus polytmus follows a defined chronology, with puberty occurring at 85 days since birth [tp = 85 days since birth] under the same active metabolic conditions of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This timing, estimated from the onset of gonadal swelling and associated testosterone surges in captive individuals, marks the point at which the immature bird becomes a reproductively viable organism capable of gametogenesis. However, actual first reproduction is deferred considerably beyond this point; the time since birth at first brood is recorded at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], a lag that reflects the complex social and energetic requirements for territory establishment and pair formation in this lekking species at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This interval between puberty and first breeding is a common pattern among hummingbirds, where young males must compete for display perches and females require sufficient fat reserves to sustain the substantial cost of egg production. The extended delay ensures that the individual has attained the adult physiological condition necessary for successful incubation of the calcareous egg and subsequent provisioning of the altricial nestling.

Adult body mass in the Red-billed Streamertail exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a characteristic feature of the species. The ultimate wet weight for females averages 4.5 grams [Wwi = 4.5 grams], with field surveys documenting a natural range from 3.0 to 6.1 grams depending on reproductive state and seasonal food abundance. Males, by contrast, attain a larger average adult mass of 5.25 grams [Wwi = 5.25 grams], with individual records spanning 4.0 to 6.5 grams. This dimorphism is especially evident in the exaggerated rectrices of the male, which contribute to the higher body mass and likely impose an aerodynamic cost during the elaborate aerial displays used in courtship. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the female's more modest mass is optimized for the energetic demands of egg production and prolonged incubation, whereas the male's larger frame supports the muscular power required for sustained hovering during territorial defense. The recorded ranges of 3.0 to 6.1 grams in females (3.0-6.1 grams) [Wwi = 3.0-6.1 grams] and 4.0 to 6.5 grams in males (4.0-6.5 grams) [Wwi = 4.0-6.5 grams] highlight substantial intraspecific plasticity in response to environmental conditions.

Reproductive output in the breeding adult bird is constrained by the small body size typical of hummingbirds. Nesting females typically lay 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], a standard clutch size among trochilids that balances the high energetic cost of egg production against the limited capacity for simultaneous parental care. Under favorable conditions, individuals may complete up to 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 3 clutches per year], representing a moderate annual reproductive investment for a bird of this size. This reproductive schedule, maintained at the typical active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], yields a maximum annual fecundity that supports population stability despite the relatively high predation rates on nests and fledglings. Maximum recorded longevity for the species is estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years], a figure derived from banding studies of related hummingbirds such as Archilochus alexandri and consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in many tropical nectarivores at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Field observations of marked individuals suggest that senescent adult mortality increases markedly after the eighth year, with only a small fraction of the population persisting to the decadal maximum.
